title: The Printing Press
content:
Around 1440, Johannes Gutenberg in Mainz, Germany, combined movable metal type, an oil-based ink, and a screw press adapted from winemaking into a practical system for printing books. His 42-line Bible, produced in the 1450s, demonstrated the technology's power.

Before the press, books were copied by hand - slow, expensive, and rare. A single manuscript could take a scribe months. Printing dropped the cost of a book dramatically and multiplied output enormously. Within about 50 years, presses across Europe had produced millions of volumes.

The consequences were profound:
- Literacy spread as books became affordable.
- Ideas traveled faster and more accurately than word-of-mouth or hand-copying allowed.
- The Protestant Reformation (from 1517) spread rapidly because pamphlets and translated Bibles could be mass-produced.
- Standardized texts helped fix spelling, build national languages, and accelerate science by letting researchers share and build on exact results.

The printing press is often cited as a key trigger of the modern era - a reminder that a breakthrough in COPYING and DISTRIBUTING information can reshape society as much as any single idea it carries. Movable type had existed earlier in East Asia; Gutenberg's innovation made it economical at scale in Europe.
